title: Strait of Hormuz & maritime chokepoint crises
question: What can historical maritime chokepoint crises teach us about reducing energy-price shocks without escalating conflict?
summary: Historical maritime disruptions (1956 Suez, 1973 Embargo, 1984–88 Tanker War, 2019 Abqaiq, and 2023–25 Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb rerouting) show that physical oil supply, tanker ton-miles, war-risk insurance, strategic reserves, refining sulfur limits, and mine-clearance clocks operate on sharply different constraints. Interventions that calm a reroutable shipping corridor fail when applied to a non-bypassable cul-de-sac.

citizenGuide.whatHappenedBefore: Major maritime energy crises include the 1956–57 Suez closure (~10.1% global oil drop), 1973–74 OAPEC embargo (~7.5% drop, prices quadrupled), 1984–88 Iran–Iraq Tanker War (451 ship attacks; US Operation Earnest Will convoys), Sept 2019 Abqaiq–Khurais strikes (5.7 mb/d offline), and 2023–25 Bab el-Mandeb/Red Sea attacks (>50% transit drop rerouted via Cape of Good Hope).
citizenGuide.whyComparable: Each crisis tests whether market buffers (inventories, pipelines, tanker rerouting, SPR/IEA stock releases, and war-risk insurance backstops) can absorb supply or transit shocks without triggering wider military escalation.
citizenGuide.whatsDifferent: Bab el-Mandeb and Suez have an oceanic detour around the Cape of Good Hope (+15 transit days), whereas the Strait of Hormuz (~20.9 mb/d oil + 11.4 Bcf/d LNG) is a single-outlet cul-de-sac where overland pipelines (Saudi Petroline + UAE ADCOP) bypass only ~4.7 mb/d of oil and 0% of LNG, and where global OPEC spare capacity sits trapped inside the Gulf.
citizenGuide.whatWorked: Coordinated IEA/SPR announcements to break precautionary hoarding in bounded outages (Jan 1991, 2011, 2022), bilateral SPR sweet-crude exchange loans (2005 Katrina, 1–4 days), Cape rerouting for Red Sea disruptions (2023–25), Saudi storage + redundant stabilization towers after Abqaiq (Sept 2019), and pairing calibrated naval defense with explicit Presidential de-escalation off-ramps (April 1988).
citizenGuide.whatFailed: Assuming naval escorts are risk-free (1987 Bridgeton mining, 1988 Operation Praying Mantis & USS Vincennes shootdown of Flight 655 killing 290 civilians; 2023–25 Operation Prosperity Guardian failing to restore Red Sea container/LNG transit), offering high-sulfur sour SPR crude to sweet-configured refiners (1991 & 2005 bid rejections), or expecting a 4.4 mb/d SPR ceiling to replace a ~16 mb/d net Hormuz blockade.
citizenGuide.howWeKnow: 2 primary government operational records (DOE SPR Quick Facts/Release History & US Navy NHHC H-Gram 018-1 on the Tanker War), 5 institutional empirical analyses (EIA World Oil Transit Chokepoints, EIA Red Sea Briefs, UNCTAD Rapid Assessment, IEA Collective Actions, CRS R42335 & IN11173), and 3 competing peer-reviewed scholarly works (Talmadge 2008, Gholz & Press 2010, Hamilton 2011).

sources.title: Closing Time: Assessing the Iranian Threat to the Strait of Hormuz
sources.author: Caitlin Talmadge
sources.locator: International Security, Vol. 33, No. 1 (Summer 2008), pp. 82–117; DOI 10.1162/isec.2008.33.1.82 (corroborated in CRS R42335 pp. 9–10)
sources.rights: Copyright 2008 Harvard College and MIT; short original paraphrase and link only.
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed military-technical model showing that if Iran deploys layered seabed mines protected by mobile coastal anti-ship cruise missiles (ASCMs) and air defenses, fragile mine-countermeasure (MCM) vessels cannot sweep until ASCMs are suppressed (9–72 days) followed by physical mine clearance (28–40 days), requiring 37 to 112 days and major onshore escalation.
sources.scopeConstraint: Models a full state A2/AD mine-and-missile campaign; operational duration depends on mine density, MCM asset readiness, and whether onshore suppression triggers wider war.

sources.title: Protecting 'The Prize': Oil and the U.S. National Interest
sources.author: Eugene Gholz and Daryl G. Press
sources.locator: Security Studies, Vol. 19, No. 3 (August 2010), pp. 453–485; DOI 10.1080/09636412.2010.505865 (abstract and core 4-mechanism argument corroborated in CRS R42335)
sources.rights: Copyright 2010 Taylor & Francis; abstract-verified scholarly paraphrase and link only.
sources.notes: Competing realist/market-adaptation interpretation arguing that four market mechanisms (inventories, OPEC spare capacity, tanker rerouting/shuttle transshipment, and price-induced demand restraint) buffered supply shocks during the 1980–88 Tanker War and justify over-the-horizon military restraint. Represented from the accessible abstract and CRS synthesis.
sources.scopeConstraint: Abstract and secondary synthesis inspected (not full paywalled text); market-buffer model assumes OPEC spare capacity and sea lanes are not simultaneously trapped behind a single closed strait.

sources.title: Historical Oil Shocks
sources.author: James D. Hamilton
sources.locator: NBER Working Paper No. 16790 (February 2011), Sections on 1956–57 Suez Crisis (pp. 9–12), 1973–74 Embargo (pp. 13–16), 1980–88 Iran-Iraq War (pp. 18–20), and 1990–91 Gulf War (pp. 20–22)
sources.rights: Copyright 2011 James D. Hamilton / NBER; open-access working paper.
sources.notes: Econometric synthesis demonstrating that because short-run oil demand elasticity is very low, physical supply drops of 7–10% (1956 Suez, 1973 Embargo, 1990 Gulf War) interact with precautionary inventory demand and expectations to produce severe price spikes and recessions.
sources.scopeConstraint: Macroeconomic quarterly/monthly analysis; does not model tactical naval MCM or per-voyage hull war-risk underwriting.

sources.title: Attacks on Saudi Oil Facilities: Effects and Responses (paired with CRS Report R42335: Iran's Threat to the Strait of Hormuz)
sources.author: Congressional Research Service (Christopher M. Blanchard et al., IN11173; Kenneth Katzman et al., R42335)
sources.locator: CRS Insight IN11173 (Sept 2019, Abqaiq/Khurais restoration & prices) and CRS Report R42335 (Jan 2012, https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R42335.html, Table 1 price series & UNCLOS transit passage)
sources.rights: U.S. Congressional Research Service work; public domain.
sources.notes: Documents the Sept 14, 2019 Abqaiq-Khurais strike (5.7 mb/d offline, 14% single-day Brent jump from $60.22 to $69.02/b) and why prices retraced within two weeks without U.S. military escalation or SPR release: Saudi Aramco drew down ~180 mb storage, swapped in heavier/sourer offshore crudes, and repaired redundant stabilization towers while sea lanes remained open.
sources.scopeConstraint: Abqaiq recovery relied on pre-built processing redundancy, stored inventories, and open maritime loading terminals—conditions absent if the Strait of Hormuz itself is blocked or non-redundant LNG trains are struck.

facts.text: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly 20.9 million barrels per day (b/d) of petroleum liquids (14.7 mb/d crude/condensate and 6.1 mb/d refined products—about 20% of global consumption) and 11.4 Bcf/d of liquefied natural gas (over 20% of global LNG trade), with 89% of its crude heading to Asian markets.

Unused overland pipeline capacity in Saudi Arabia (the East-West Petroline to Yanbu on the Red Sea) and the UAE (the Habshan–Fujairah ADCOP pipeline to the Gulf of Oman) can bypass only ~4.7 million b/d of oil during a Hormuz disruption, leaving ~16 million b/d of oil and 100% of Qatari LNG without an overland or oceanic detour.

facts.text: During the 2023–2025 Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb shipping attacks, Bab el-Mandeb oil flows fell by more than half (from 9.3 mb/d to 4.1–4.2 mb/d) and LNG transits fell to zero, while oil rerouted around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope surged ~50% (from 5.9–6.2 mb/d to 8.7–9.3 mb/d), adding ~15 voyage days to Europe and +20% clean tanker freight rates while Brent crude spot prices stayed stable ($82/b to $79/b in early 2024).

facts.text: The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has a maximum physical drawdown ceiling of 4.4 million barrels per day and a 13-day lag from Presidential decision to market pipeline entry. In the January 1991 Desert Storm sale (17.3 mb bought of 33.75 mb offered) and September 2005 Katrina sale (11.0 mb bought of 30 mb offered), U.S. refiners rejected nearly half of offered SPR barrels because they required low-sulfur 'sweet' crude rather than high-sulfur 'sour' crude.

During the 1984–1988 Iran–Iraq Tanker War (451 merchant vessels attacked through 1987), the U.S. Navy reflagged 11 Kuwaiti tankers under Operation Earnest Will. While Gulf oil exports continued and global crude prices fell (-9.6% in the month after the July 24, 1987 Bridgeton mining), mine strikes on Bridgeton and USS Samuel B. Roberts (April 14, 1988) triggered Operation Praying Mantis (April 18, 1988) and expanded surface-warfare rules of engagement under which USS Vincennes mistakenly shot down Iran Air Flight 655 on July 3, 1988, killing 290 civilians.

facts.text: Following the September 14, 2019 drone and cruise-missile strikes on Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq stabilization plant and Khurais field (knocking out 5.7 mb/d, or ~5% of world oil supply, and spiking Brent 14% on Sept 16), prices returned near pre-attack levels within two weeks without U.S. military retaliation or an SPR release because Aramco tapped ~180 million barrels in storage, substituted heavier/sourer offshore crudes, and repaired redundant stabilization towers while sea lanes stayed open.

timeline.title: Suez Canal blockage & IPC sabotage
timeline.text: Blockage of the Suez Canal and Iraq Petroleum Company pipelines removed ~10.1% of world oil output, forcing tanker rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope until diplomatic withdrawal.

timeline.title: OAPEC oil embargo & creation of IEA/SPR
timeline.text: OAPEC production cuts (~7.5% of global output) quadrupled oil prices in the absence of strategic stocks, prompting the creation of the IEA (1974) and U.S. SPR (1975).

timeline.title: Operation Earnest Will, Praying Mantis & Flight 655
timeline.text: Reflagged Kuwaiti convoys preserved Gulf oil transit alongside 17 coalition minesweepers, but mine hits led to Operation Praying Mantis (April 1988) and the tragic shootdown of Iran Air Flight 655 (July 1988).

timeline.title: Desert Storm & first IEA/SPR release
timeline.text: Coordinated IEA/SPR announcement calmed precautionary war-premium hoarding within hours, 20 days before first physical SPR delivery on Feb 5, 1991 (refiners bought 17.3 mb of 33.75 mb offered, rejecting sour crude).

timeline.title: Abqaiq–Khurais processing strike (5.7 mb/d)
timeline.text: Strikes knocked out half of Saudi output (+14% opening Brent spike), but Saudi storage (~180 mb), crude grade swaps, and redundant stabilization towers restored supply in two weeks without military escalation.

timeline.title: Bab el-Mandeb attacks & Cape rerouting
timeline.text: Bab el-Mandeb oil transits fell >50% (9.3 to 4.1–4.2 mb/d) and LNG fell to zero; Cape of Good Hope rerouting (+15 days) kept Brent spot stable ($82 to $79/b) while naval escorts alone could not restore Red Sea container/LNG traffic.

comparison.historical: In 2023–2025 Bab el-Mandeb attacks, cutting Red Sea oil transit by >50% (from 9.3 to 4.1–4.2 mb/d) did not reduce global wellhead supply; tankers diverted around the Cape of Good Hope (+15 transit days PG-to-Rotterdam), raising clean freight rates 20% while Brent spot prices held near $79–$82/b.
comparison.present: As of 2026-11-08, evaluate whether a chokepoint crisis blocks a reroutable passage (like Bab el-Mandeb/Suez) or a single-outlet cul-de-sac (like the Strait of Hormuz, ~20.9 mb/d oil + 11.4 Bcf/d LNG), where overland pipelines (Petroline + ADCOP) bypass only ~4.7 mb/d of oil and 0% of LNG.
comparison.limit: Cape of Good Hope rerouting works ONLY for Bab el-Mandeb and Suez; it cannot bypass the Strait of Hormuz, where >75% of oil flow and 100% of Qatari LNG have no maritime or overland detour.
comparison.timeframe: 15–21 Days (fleet Cape rerouting equilibration) vs. 7–30 Days (ramping existing 4.7 mb/d pipeline bypass) vs. Years (building new pipelines)

comparison.dimension: War-risk insurance, naval escorts & mine-clearance clocks
comparison.historical: In Operation Earnest Will (1987–88), reflagging 11 Kuwaiti tankers and deploying 17 coalition minesweepers maintained transit, but Bridgeton hit a mine on the first convoy (July 1987), USS Samuel B. Roberts hit a mine (April 1988), and combat escalated into Operation Praying Mantis and the July 1988 USS Vincennes shootdown of Iran Air Flight 655 (290 killed).
comparison.present: As of 2026-11-08, separate commercial hull/cargo war-risk repricing or P&I coverage withdrawal (24–72 hours) from the military-technical clock required to suppress mobile coastal anti-ship cruise missiles (9–72 days) and sweep naval mines (28–40 days, totaling 37–112 days per Talmadge 2008).
comparison.limit: Defensive naval escorts cannot safely operate inside a dense minefield or under shore-based ASCM/drone saturation without suppressing onshore batteries—which crosses the threshold into direct state-on-state war—unless paired with pre-positioned MCM assets and an explicit diplomatic off-ramp.
comparison.timeframe: 24–72 Hours (commercial war-risk repricing/withdrawal) · 3–7 Days (carrier/escort surge) · 37–112 Days (9–72d ASCM suppression + 28–40d mine clearance)

rejectedComparisons.claim: Because global crude oil prices stayed stable (~$79–$82/b) during the 2023–2025 Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb attacks, global oil markets will similarly shrug off a Strait of Hormuz closure through tanker rerouting and market adaptation.
rejectedComparisons.whyItFails: Treats a pass-through strait with an oceanic detour (Bab el-Mandeb/Suez via the Cape of Good Hope, +15 transit days) as equivalent to a cul-de-sac sea outlet (Strait of Hormuz). Hormuz has zero sea detour, overland pipelines (Petroline + ADCOP) can bypass only ~4.7 mb/d of its 20.9 mb/d oil flow and 0% of its 11.4 Bcf/d LNG flow, and global OPEC spare capacity sits trapped inside the Persian Gulf.
rejectedComparisons.counterEvidence: EIA World Oil Transit Chokepoints (`hormuz-eia-chokepoints`) and EIA Red Sea Briefs (`hormuz-eia-redsea`) showing Cape flows absorbing 100% of diverted Red Sea oil vs. <25% overland pipeline bypass for Hormuz.

rejectedComparisons.claim: Releasing the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve and deploying naval convoy escorts on the 1987 Operation Earnest Will model guarantees a rapid, non-escalatory resolution to a Strait of Hormuz blockade.
rejectedComparisons.whyItFails: Violates two hard physical and operational constraints: (1) The U.S. SPR's maximum physical drawdown rate is capped at 4.4 mb/d (with a 13-day auction pipeline lag and sour-crude refining limits) and 0 Bcf/d for LNG, which cannot replace a ~16 mb/d net Hormuz deficit; (2) Earnest Will faced limited contact mines yet still suffered the Bridgeton and Roberts mine strikes, escalated into Operation Praying Mantis, and culminated in the Iran Air Flight 655 tragedy (290 killed), while clearing a modern ASCM-defended minefield requires 37–112 days of onshore suppression and MCM sweeping (Talmadge 2008).
rejectedComparisons.counterEvidence: DOE SPR Quick Facts (`hormuz-doe-spr`), NHHC Tanker War command history (`hormuz-nhhc-tanker-war`), and Talmadge 2008 (`hormuz-talmadge-2008`).

outcomes.text: Documented outcome (1984–88 Tanker War & Earnest Will): Reflagging 11 Kuwaiti tankers, deploying 17 coalition minesweepers, Larak shuttle tankers, and pipeline expansion kept Gulf exports flowing and prices falling (-9.6% after July 1987), but compressed naval rules of engagement led to Operation Praying Mantis (April 1988) and the mistaken USS Vincennes shootdown of Iran Air Flight 655 (290 civilians killed, July 1988). Presidential de-escalation orders (halting the Rakhsh platform strike and sparing the frigate Sabalan) were required to prevent wider war before UNSCR 598.
confounders: 1980s global OPEC spare capacity glut outside immediate attack zones
Simultaneous expansion of Saudi Petroline and Iraqi pipelines through Turkey
Diplomatic exhaustion leading to UNSCR 598 acceptance in July 1988
outcomes.counterfactualGap: Price stability during 1987–88 cannot be credited to naval escorts alone given the 1980s global oil glut and shuttle-tanker adaptations.

outcomes.text: Documented outcome (1991, 2005, 2011, 2022 SPR & IEA Releases): Announcing the Jan 16, 1991 IEA/SPR release alongside Desert Storm air strikes broke precautionary hoarding within hours—20 days before first physical SPR delivery on Feb 5—and 2005 bilateral SPR exchange loans bridged Katrina refinery outages in 1–4 days. However, in both 1991 (17.3 mb sold of 33.75 mb offered) and 2005 (0.2 mb sour vs. 10.8 mb sweet sold), refiners rejected nearly half of offered SPR barrels due to high-sulfur sour crude mismatch.
confounders: Simultaneous Jan 16–17, 1991 Allied air supremacy confirming Saudi oil fields were safe from Iraqi attack
Saudi Arabian production surge offsetting Kuwaiti/Iraqi losses
outcomes.counterfactualGap: The Jan 1991 price collapse occurred before physical SPR oil moved, making it impossible to separate the IEA announcement effect from battlefield news that Saudi terminals were secure.

outcomes.text: Documented outcome (Sept 2019 Abqaiq–Khurais & 2023–25 Red Sea): After the Sept 14, 2019 strike knocked out 5.7 mb/d, military restraint combined with Saudi Aramco's ~180 mb storage drawdown, sourer crude grade swaps, and redundant stabilization towers reversed a 14% price spike within two weeks. In 2023–25, Cape of Good Hope rerouting (+15 days) prevented a global crude price spike during Bab el-Mandeb attacks, even as Operation Prosperity Guardian naval patrols failed to restore Red Sea LNG (0 Bcf/d) or container (-82%) transit.
confounders: Global demand softness in late 2019 and 2024
Availability of open maritime loading terminals in Sept 2019 and the Cape of Good Hope detour in 2023–25
outcomes.counterfactualGap: Neither case tested an outright closure of the Strait of Hormuz where sea lanes and spare capacity are blocked simultaneously.

counterexamples.title: 1991 & 2005 SPR sour-crude bid rejections
counterexamples.text: In January 1991, DOE offered 33.75 million barrels from the SPR, but refiners purchased only 17.3 million barrels (and only 0.2 mb of sour crude in the Sept 2005 Katrina sale) because U.S. refineries lacked available desulfurization capacity for high-sulfur sour crude.
counterexamples.failureCondition: Headline strategic reserve volumes overstate usable supply when released crude grades do not match downstream refinery sulfur and API gravity limits.

counterexamples.title: July 1987 Bridgeton mining, April 1988 Praying Mantis & July 1988 Flight 655 tragedy
counterexamples.text: On the very first Operation Earnest Will convoy (July 24, 1987), the reflagged supertanker Bridgeton struck an Iranian contact mine and had to lead its warship escorts out of the Gulf; ten months later, mine strikes escalated into Operation Praying Mantis and the USS Vincennes shootdown of Iran Air Flight 655 (290 killed).
counterexamples.failureCondition: Naval escorting without prior mine-countermeasure superiority and strict de-escalation guardrails triggers direct combat and severe collateral tragedy.

counterexamples.title: 2023–2025 Operation Prosperity Guardian vs. commercial insurer & carrier avoidance
counterexamples.text: Despite a 20+ nation naval escort coalition in the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb LNG transit fell to 0.0 Bcf/d in 2024–1H25 and Suez container tonnage dropped 82% as war-risk premiums rose ~900%.
counterexamples.failureCondition: Defensive warship patrols alone cannot restore commercial transit against low-cost onshore drones and missiles when commercial underwriters and shipowners refuse hull/crew exposure.

interpretations.title: Market adaptation & over-the-horizon restraint (Gholz & Press 2010 — Abstract & CRS synthesis)
interpretations.text: Gholz and Press argue that global oil markets possess four adaptive buffers—commercial/public inventories, OPEC spare capacity, tanker rerouting/shuttle transshipment, and price-induced demand restraint—that absorbed the 1980–88 Tanker War and justify an over-the-horizon U.S. military posture rather than hair-trigger intervention. (Note: Represented from the published Security Studies abstract and CRS R42335 synthesis; full paywalled article not bundled.)
interpretations.causalEmphasis: Market adaptation via inventories, spare capacity, and tanker rerouting (Abstract/synthesis only)

survivingTextByWithdrawnSource.hormuz-gholz-press-2010: Surviving institutional synthesis (`hormuz-crs-abqaiq-2019`): With the abstract-only `hormuz-gholz-press-2010` card withdrawn/reopened, CRS Report R42335 (`hormuz-crs-abqaiq-2019`) independently documents the 1984–88 Tanker War price decline and market-buffer mechanisms while explicitly noting the ~4.7 mb/d pipeline bypass ceiling.

interpretations.title: Military-technical A2/AD & mine-clearance bottleneck (Talmadge 2008)
interpretations.text: Talmadge contends that analogies to 1980s tanker harassment ignore modern layered anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) capabilities: because fragile mine-countermeasure (MCM) ships and helicopters cannot operate under mobile coastal anti-ship cruise missile (ASCM) and air-defense fire, reopening a mined Strait of Hormuz requires 9–72 days of onshore suppression plus 28–40 days of physical mine sweeping (37–112 days total).
interpretations.causalEmphasis: Military-technical mine-countermeasure (MCM) and coastal ASCM suppression timeline bottleneck

interpretations.title: Short-run demand inelasticity & precautionary expectation shocks (Hamilton 2011)
interpretations.text: Hamilton demonstrates econometrically across the 1956, 1973, 1979, and 1990 oil shocks that because short-run price elasticity of oil demand is extremely low, modest physical flow disruptions (7–10% of world supply) interact with precautionary inventory hoarding to cause nonlinear price spikes and recessions—making rapid, credible 0–72 hour reserve/repair signaling vital, yet insufficient if physical blockage outlasts stock drawdown ceilings.
interpretations.causalEmphasis: Macroeconomic demand inelasticity and precautionary inventory/futures amplification

consequentialCorrection.targetSourceTitle: Eugene Gholz & Daryl G. Press, 'Protecting The Prize' (Security Studies, 2010 — Abstract Only)
consequentialCorrection.challengeReason: Source `hormuz-gholz-press-2010` is curated from an abstract/secondary synthesis (`ABSTRACT_ONLY`) and its market-adaptation thesis assumes OPEC spare capacity and tanker rerouting remain accessible—an assumption that breaks in a full Strait of Hormuz closure where spare capacity is trapped inside the Persian Gulf.
consequentialCorrection.expectedImpact: Challenging or withdrawing `hormuz-gholz-press-2010` reopens 4 dependent records (`hormuz-facts-5`, `hormuz-comparison-3`, `hormuz-outcomes-1`, `hormuz-interpretations-1`), each of which displays its surviving primary/institutional fallback basis (`hormuz-nhhc-tanker-war`, `hormuz-crs-abqaiq-2019`, `hormuz-eia-chokepoints`), while leaving all 16 other records in Case A `AVAILABLE`.

limits: No historical maritime crisis is a predictive guarantee: a mechanism that stabilized prices during a reroutable Red Sea disruption (2023–25) or a low-intensity tanker harassment campaign during a global glut (1984–88) cannot be promised to work during a full Strait of Hormuz closure.
Overland pipelines (Saudi Petroline + UAE ADCOP) can bypass only ~4.7 mb/d of the ~20.9 mb/d of oil transiting Hormuz, and 0% of the 11.4 Bcf/d of Qatari LNG.

The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is bounded by a 4.4 million b/d physical drawdown ceiling, a 13-day auction/pipeline delivery lag, and sweet-vs-sour refinery sulfur constraints; no strategic reserve exists globally for LNG.
Gholz & Press (2010) is represented from its published abstract and CRS R42335 synthesis (`ABSTRACT_ONLY`), not a bundled full-text reprint.
Contemporary flow baselines are dated and sourced as of 2026-11-08 from EIA, DOE, IEA, and UNCTAD records.
challengePrompts: Why did a >50% drop in Bab el-Mandeb oil transits in 2024 leave Brent crude near $79–$82/b, and why does that Cape of Good Hope rerouting mechanism fail for the Strait of Hormuz?
Under what outage size (in mb/d) and duration (in days) do the ~4.7 mb/d pipeline bypass and the 4.4 mb/d U.S. SPR drawdown ceiling become mathematically insufficient?
Why did U.S. refiners reject nearly half of the SPR crude offered during the 1991 Desert Storm and 2005 Katrina drawdowns?
What operational sequence explains why naval minesweepers cannot immediately clear a strait defended by mobile coastal anti-ship missiles?

questionProfile.primaryDomain: Strait of Hormuz, maritime energy chokepoints, strategic reserves, naval convoys & oil shocks
questionProfile.whyRelevantSummary: The Strait of Hormuz & Maritime Chokepoint dossier (1956–2026) examines what history establishes about prolonged maritime energy disruptions: physical flow and pipeline bypass limits (~20.9 mb/d oil and 11.4 Bcf/d LNG vs. ~4.7 mb/d overland crude pipeline bypass and 0 Bcf/d LNG bypass), why the 2023–2025 Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope (+15 transit days) does not transfer to the Persian Gulf cul-de-sac, what Strategic Petroleum Reserve drawdowns and 1987–1988 Operation Earnest Will naval convoys achieved, and where those interventions hit hard physical or escalation limits.
supportedThemes: Physical topology and bypass ceilings in a prolonged Strait of Hormuz disruption (~20.9 mb/d oil, 11.4 Bcf/d LNG, ~4.7 mb/d pipeline bypass, 0 LNG reserve/bypass)
Why Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb oceanic rerouting (2023–2025) and the 2019 Abqaiq-Khurais storage/spare-capacity buffer fail as analogies for a full Hormuz closure

Competing military-technical (Talmadge 2008: 37–112 days MCM + ASCM suppression) vs. market-adaptation (Gholz & Press 2010) and macroeconomic (Hamilton 2011) arguments, plus 1987–88 Earnest Will escalation hazards
knownCoverageGaps: Does not cover Malacca Strait or Taiwan Strait semiconductor/container blockades, cyber-only grid attacks, or post-2026 pipeline construction
Gholz & Press (2010) is represented from its accessible abstract and CRS synthesis rather than a full-text journal reprint

historicalArguments.topic: 1980–1988 Tanker War market adaptation & convoy protection vs. modern layered mine/ASCM denial
historicalArguments.decisionWindow: 1987–1988 Operation Earnest Will vs. 2008–2012 Hormuz Closure Debates
historicalArguments.contemporaryActor: U.S. Naval Command (1987–88) & later strategic analysts Caitlin Talmadge (2008) vs. Eugene Gholz & Daryl G. Press (2010)
historicalArguments.contemporaryArgument: During 1987–1988 Operation Earnest Will, U.S. policymakers argued that reflagging Kuwaiti tankers and escorting convoys with U.S. warships would deter mines and small-boat attacks and keep Gulf oil flowing. In subsequent strategic debates, Gholz & Press (2010 abstract/CRS synthesis) argued that four market adaptations (inventories, OPEC spare capacity, shuttle tankers, and price restraint) buffered the 1980–88 Tanker War, whereas Talmadge (2008) argued that modern layered seabed mines backed by mobile coastal anti-ship cruise missiles (ASCMs) and air defenses create an asymmetric denial problem unlike 1987–88.
historicalArguments.policymakerExpectation: 1987 policymakers expected naval escorts to maintain transit with manageable risk, while market-adaptation proponents expected commercial rerouting and spare capacity to absorb maritime harassment without major onshore war.
historicalArguments.subsequentEvidence: Operation Earnest Will preserved Kuwaiti tanker transit during 1987–88, but immediately hit acute operational and escalation limits: reflagged supertanker MV Bridgeton struck a moored contact mine on the very first convoy (24 July 1987) when U.S. forces lacked in-theater mine-countermeasure (MCM) ships; USS Samuel B. Roberts struck a mine on 14 April 1988, triggering the surface combat of Operation Praying Mantis (18 April 1988); and USS Vincennes shot down civilian Iran Air Flight 655 on 3 July 1988, killing 290 passengers and crew (hormuz-nhhc-tanker-war). Furthermore, Talmadge's technical model shows fragile MCM sweepers cannot operate until mobile coastal ASCMs are suppressed onshore (9–72 days) followed by 28–40 days of mine sweeping (37–112 days total) (hormuz-talmadge-2008).
historicalArguments.laterHistoriography: Naval historians (hormuz-nhhc-tanker-war) and security scholars (hormuz-talmadge-2008 vs. hormuz-gholz-press-2010) distinguish episodic 1980s tanker harassment (~1–2% of transits hit while the strait stayed open) from a concerted modern mine-and-missile closure where Gulf OPEC spare capacity is trapped upstream of the chokepoint.
historicalArguments.differenceThatLimits: 1987–88 Iraq-Iran anti-shipping attacks used sparse moored mines and unguided rockets without attempting to close the entire Strait of Hormuz using modern acoustic/magnetic mines and mobile coastal ASCM batteries.

Roberts mine strikes, escalated into Operation Praying Mantis and Iran Air Flight 655, and that clearing a modern layered mine-and-ASCM denial requires 37–112 days.

historicalArguments.topic: Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) & IEA stock releases vs. prolonged Hormuz oil and LNG shut-in
historicalArguments.decisionWindow: 1991 Desert Storm, 2005 Katrina, 2011 Libya & 2022 Ukraine Collective Releases
historicalArguments.contemporaryActor: U.S. Department of Energy (SPR) & International Energy Agency (IEA) Governing Board
historicalArguments.contemporaryArgument: Energy officials argued during the 1991, 2005, 2011, and 2022 crises that coordinated public stock drawdowns and reduced industry stockholding obligations could bridge temporary supply disruptions, calm precautionary hoarding, and restrain spot price spikes (hormuz-doe-spr, hormuz-iea-releases).
historicalArguments.policymakerExpectation: Policymakers expected emergency SPR exchange loans (1–4 days) and competitive sales (13 days to enter pipelines/barges) to substitute for lost crude barrels during short-duration outages while markets adjusted.
historicalArguments.subsequentEvidence: Coordinated IEA/SPR releases calmed short-term market panic in 1991 and 2022, but historical operational records expose three hard physical ceilings against a prolonged Hormuz closure: (1) U.S. SPR drawdown is physically capped at a nominal 4.4 million b/d maximum rate with a 13-day competitive sale delivery lag vs. ~20.9 mb/d of Hormuz oil flow (~16.2 mb/d net after ~4.7 mb/d Saudi Petroline and UAE ADCOP pipeline bypass); (2) in 1991 (17.3 mb sold of 33.75 mb offered) and 2005 (11.0 mb sold of 30 mb offered), refiners rejected higher-sulfur sour SPR crude when they needed light sweet grades; and (3) neither the U.S. nor IEA holds any strategic reserve for the 11.4 Bcf/d of Qatari/UAE Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) transiting Hormuz (~20% of global LNG trade) (hormuz-eia-chokepoints, hormuz-doe-spr, hormuz-iea-releases).
historicalArguments.laterHistoriography: Econometric research by James D. Hamilton (hormuz-hamilton-2011) alongside DOE/IEA operational histories (hormuz-doe-spr, hormuz-iea-releases) shows that because short-run oil demand elasticity is extremely low, net physical supply losses exceeding reserve and pipeline rate ceilings trigger nonlinear precautionary inventory spikes and macroeconomic contraction.
historicalArguments.differenceThatLimits: Strategic crude reserves designed for 30-to-180-day partial outages cannot physically replace ~16.2 mb/d of net unbypassed Gulf oil or 11.4 Bcf/d of unbypassed LNG.

historicalArguments.topic: 2019 Abqaiq repair & 2023–2025 Red Sea Cape rerouting vs. Persian Gulf geographic cul-de-sac
historicalArguments.decisionWindow: September 2019 (Abqaiq-Khurais Strike) & 2023–2025 (Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb Rerouting)
historicalArguments.contemporaryActor: Market commentators vs. EIA, UNCTAD & Congressional Research Service analysts
historicalArguments.contemporaryArgument: After the September 14, 2019 Abqaiq-Khurais strike briefly knocked out 5.7 mb/d and after 2023–2025 Houthi Red Sea attacks cut Bab el-Mandeb oil transits by over 50% without causing a sustained global oil price spike, some commentators argued that modern global energy markets can similarly shrug off or reroute around a Strait of Hormuz closure.
historicalArguments.policymakerExpectation: Optimistic market observers expected tanker fleet rerouting and Saudi/OPEC spare capacity to cushion any Middle Eastern maritime disruption much as they did in September 2019 and 2023–2025.
historicalArguments.subsequentEvidence: Institutional data from EIA, UNCTAD, and CRS prove why both analogies fail structurally for a Strait of Hormuz closure: (1) during the 2023–2025 Red Sea disruption, Bab el-Mandeb functioned as a pass-through canal where tankers diverted around the Cape of Good Hope (surging ~50% from 5.9–6.2 mb/d to 8.7–9.3 mb/d, adding ~15 transit days from 19 to 35 days PG-to-Rotterdam and +20% clean tanker rates while keeping barrels on the water), whereas the Persian Gulf is a geographic cul-de-sac with zero oceanic detour (hormuz-eia-redsea, hormuz-unctad-redsea, hormuz-eia-chokepoints); and (2) after the Sept 2019 Abqaiq strike, prices retraced within two weeks only because Persian Gulf sea lanes and terminals remained open while Saudi Aramco drew down ~180 mb of storage—whereas a Hormuz closure traps Gulf export terminals and upstream OPEC spare capacity inside the Gulf once ~4.7 mb/d of pipeline bypass is full (hormuz-crs-abqaiq-2019, hormuz-eia-chokepoints).
historicalArguments.laterHistoriography: Energy economists and maritime analysts (hormuz-eia-chokepoints, hormuz-eia-redsea, hormuz-unctad-redsea, hormuz-crs-abqaiq-2019) distinguish transit-elongation shocks (Bab el-Mandeb/Suez) and inland processing outages with open ports (Abqaiq 2019) from origin-chokepoint shut-ins (Hormuz).
historicalArguments.differenceThatLimits: A pass-through maritime corridor with an oceanic detour around Africa (Bab el-Mandeb) is topologically opposite to a semi-enclosed sea (Persian Gulf) where 89% of crude exports head to Asia and pipelines bypass less than 25% of oil and 0% of LNG.

survivingTextByWithdrawnSource.hormuz-unctad-redsea: EIA chokepoint and Red Sea flow records (hormuz-eia-chokepoints, hormuz-eia-redsea) and CRS Abqaiq analysis (hormuz-crs-abqaiq-2019) establish that Bab el-Mandeb traffic diverted around the Cape of Good Hope (+15 transit days) and Abqaiq relied on open Gulf export terminals, whereas Hormuz is a geographic cul-de-sac with ~4.7 mb/d pipeline bypass and 0% LNG bypass.
